Learning Objectives
Assess the natural history of cruciate ligament injuries in young patients.
Identify relevant anatomic features of cruciate injuries in skeletally immature patients.
Define age-based treatment options for anterior cruciate ligament injuries in skeletally
immature patients.

Definition: rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) with resultant pain, instability, and
dysfunction in a young patient with ongoing skeletal growth and maturation

Overview
ACL ruptures may affect skeletally immature patients and are becoming increasingly
more common. The role of the ACL in controlling anterior-posterior translation and
rotation of the knee during activity has been well documented. ACL rupture may allow
for excess movement and rotation of the knee during activity, leading to secondary
injuries and degeneration of the knee joint.1
Epidemiology
A three-fold increase in ACL reconstruction surgical procedures was reported in patients
younger than 20 years between 1990 and 2009.
Although previously occurring at low rates in adolescents, currently, this patient population
represents the largest per capita demographic for ACL reconstruction.
The incidence of ACL reconstruction in patients younger than 20 years likely is the result of the
changing culture in adolescent sports.

Epidemiology
In an epidemiologic analysis of 25,000 children aged 3 to 20 years, Dodwell et al2
reported that the rate of ACL reconstruction per 100,000 individuals was 17.6% in 1990
and increased to 50.9% in 2009, an overall threefold increase in occurrence. A separate
study reported that ambulatory ACL procedures in patients younger than 15 years
increased 924% between 1994 and 2006.3 ACL tears in youth populations were originally
thought to be uncommon because of greater strength of the ligament over open physes,
and these injuries were commonly managed nonsurgically until skeletal maturity.4
Subsequent studies found that nonsurgical management of ACL injuries in young
patients led to poor outcomes and secondary articular damage, such as meniscal tears

and cartilage injury/degeneration.5 The drastic rise in ACL reconstruction in patients
younger than 20 years may be to the result of a shift in youth competitive athletic
activity, with an increase in early sport specialization and year-round
training/competition.
Anatomy/Pathoanatomy
The ACL originates on the intercondylar notch of the lateral femoral condyle and inserts on the
central tibial plateau. It consists of two bundles: anteromedial and posterolateral.
Skeletal maturation must be accounted for during ACL reconstruction because surgical
reconstruction may lead to physeal injury and/or arrest.
Common concomitant injuries that occur in combination with ACL rupture include meniscal
and cartilage injury.

Anatomy/Pathoanatomy
The ACL originates on the medial side of the lateral femoral condyle and runs obliquely
across the center of the knee, inserting on the central tibial plateau.1 The ACL consists of
two bundles, the anteromedial bundle and the posterolateral bundle, named for the
locations they implant on the tibial plateau. The anteromedial and posterolateral
bundles are necessary for normal function of the ACL because they play distinct roles.1
The anteromedial bundle generally is believed to be isometric throughout knee range of
motion. The exception to this rule involves the anterior-most fibers, which relax-just
before terminal extension to prevent impingement on the intercondylar notch. Because
of its insertion site and isometry, the anteromedial bundle is believed to be the primary
restraint to anterior translation of the proximal tibia throughout knee range of motion.6
It also supplies ancillary support against internal and external rotation forces.7 The
posterolateral bundle fibers are anisometric at varying degrees of knee flexion. During
flexion, the posterolateral bundle wraps around the anteromedial bundle at the femur.8
The posterolateral bundle fibers are parallel and completely taut in full extension. The
posterolateral bundle fibers gradually relax during flexion until 90°, at which point they
again become tensioned. Because of its insertion site and anisometric tension, the

posterolateral bundle aids in regulating anterior translation in extension and is the
principal restraint to tibial rotation at the extents of extension and flexion.6,9
The distal femoral and proximal tibial physes are relevant concerns in evaluating ACL
injuries in growing children. Growth from the distal femur occurs at a rate of 9 mm/yr,
whereas the proximal tibia grows at a mean rate of 6 mm/yr.10 Minimal growth (<1 cm
per limb segment) remains about the knee after age 12 or 13 years in girls (ie, 1 year
after menarche) and age 14 in boys.11 During ACL injury, the lateral distal femur and the
posterior proximal tibia collide during the pivot shift mechanism of injury, and the
resultant osseous injury is commonly observed as a bone bruise pattern on MRI.
Novaretti et al12 showed that the bony changes are largely confined to the epiphysis in
skeletally immature patients, suggesting that the physes play a role in force dissipation
in these injuries. This finding suggests that ACL injuries may lead to direct injury to the
adjacent physes in addition to the risk associated with surgical management.
As ACL injuries commonly result from high-impact situations, concomitant injuries are
common. Vavken et al13 reported that more than one-half of patients younger than 18
years who underwent ACL surgery had a concurrent meniscal or chondral injury. In that
series, 32% and 35% of patients had medial and lateral meniscus tears, respectively, and
5% of patients had chondral lesions requiring management. This confirmed previous
reports of high school athletes with ACL injuries and meniscal and cartilage injury rates
of 57% and 20%, respectively.14
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Each encounter should begin with a thorough patient history and physical examination.
In female athletes, documentation of menarche is important to help guide treatment.
Initial physical examination includes Lachman, anterior drawer, and pivot shift tests; however,
physicians also should evaluate clinical malalignment and leg-length discrepancy.


Patient History and Physical Examination
Each encounter should begin with a thorough patient history and physical examination,
ruling out concomitant injury. Historical features to collect are similar to those obtained
during the evaluation of older patients with an ACL injury (injury history, athletic
participation, knee-specific symptoms); however, specific determination and
documentation of menstrual history for females is especially important in young
athletes. Menarche has been endorsed in numerous studies as being associated with
deceleration of skeletal growth and progression toward skeletal maturity in females.15-18
On physical examination, ACL injuries are present in as many as 65% of adolescents with
acute traumatic hemarthrosis.19 Lachman, anterior drawer, and pivot shift tests may
detect ACL insufficiency; however, pain and swelling may affect patient compliance and
the accuracy of these tests. The pivot shift test is positive in as many as 98% of
anesthetized patients, whereas it is positive in as few as 35% of awake patients.19,20
Surgeons must evaluate for baseline clinical malalignment of the lower extremities,
especially assessing for pathologic states of genu valgum or leg-length discrepancy.
Tanner staging and assessment of secondary sexual development is appropriate in these
individuals but is not widely implemented during clinical encounters.
Imaging Studies
Radiography and MRI are necessary to fully characterize the injury and determine a safe
means of treatment.
Radiography allows for a comprehensive understanding of bone age and expected skeletal
development, which must be accounted for.
MRI allows for visualization of the ACL along with other soft-tissue structures that must be
assessed in patients with an ACL injury.

Despite numerous studies on reconstruction management techniques for pediatric ACL
tears, to date, no standardized consensus exists on the diagnostic work up of ACL tears
in skeletally immature patients. Radiography is useful to determine necessary skeletal
measurements, such as leg length and bone age, whereas MRI is useful for visualization
of the ligament injury and other potential soft-tissue injuries commonly associated with
ACL rupture.
Radiography
Radiography is vital to injury assessment and surgical planning for ACL rupture.
Radiographs are used to assess preexisting deformities, differences in leg lengths, and bone
age (Figure 1).


Radiography
No standardized consensus exists with regard to radiographs necessary for correct
assessment of ACL injuries in the skeletally immature population. Knee-specific
radiographs, including some combination of AP, lateral, and flexion (tunnel or notch)
views, are routinely obtained in older patients with an ACL injury. In addition, for
skeletally immature individuals, long-leg alignment and bone age (left hand) views
should be considered.
Alignment and bone age radiographs allow for preoperative characterization of
preexisting deformities and provide reliable means of projecting future growth. Long-leg
alignment radiographs identify preexisting angular deformities that may contribute to
increased graft strain (specifically genu valgum), and are important to follow over time to
monitor for growth disturbances.21,22 This information can enable deformity correction
via guided growth or osteotomy at the time of index ACL management and allows for
longitudinal observation of growth after management. Skeletal age, assessed via a
radiograph of the left hand, provides an image-based estimation of skeletal growth
remaining and may differ from chronologic age in adolescents.23 Calculation of skeletal
age provides a meaningful tool for the surgical decision-making process with regard to
the surgical approach, technique, and graft choice.24,25
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the most specific imaging modality because of its ability to evaluate ligamentous injury
and, more specifically, the ACL (Figure 2).
MRI allows for evaluation of common concomitant injuries, such as meniscal, cartilage, and
other ligamentous injuries.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the standard imaging modality to detect an ACL injury, and is 95% sensitive and
88% specific with regard to the diagnosis of ACL tears in children.26 MRI allows for
visualization of the ACL in combination with other articular structures about the knee
that are at risk in ACL-deficient athletes, including the menisci, articular cartilage, the
medial collateral ligament, and structures of the posterolateral corner. It also allows for
visualization of lateral-sided bone bruise patterns typical in patients with an ACL rupture.
Because meniscal and cartilage injury have been observed in more than one-half of high
school athletes with an ACL injury, surgeons also must assess for these injuries.13,14

Management
Overview
Nonsurgical management involves strict activity modifications and physical rehabilitation, with
or without functional bracing, to avoid repetitive injuries to the ACL-deficient knee.
Nonsurgical management of ACL injuries in skeletally immature individuals leads to
predictable injury and degeneration of other knee structures, including the menisci and
articular cartilage
Surgical management is indicated for most ACL ruptures in skeletally immature patients given
the complications associated with nonsurgical management.
An age-based approach should be used to determine the best surgical approach for ACL
injuries in skeletally immature patients.

Overview
Nonsurgical management of ACL injuries in skeletally immature individuals was
historically endorsed given the supposed healing potential of children and the risk of
physeal damage with surgical reconstruction; however, clinical healing rarely occurred,
with subsequent reports indicating that nonsurgical management led to considerable
sport dropout (as many as 94% unable to participate at preinjury level of activity and as
many as 50% unable to participate at all) because of recurrent, symptomatic
instability.5,27-29 In addition, continued instability events may result in progressive
meniscal and cartilage damage and arthritic changes in 61% of knees.5,29-31 Several
studies have shown increasing frequency of cartilage and meniscal damage with
instability episodes in the young, ACL-deficient knees. Anderson and Anderson32 noted
2.2-times and 3.5-times higher risk of lateral and medial meniscus injury, respectively,
with management delayed more than 12 weeks. Moksnes et al28 performed a large,
prospective MRI-based study that advocated against the routine reconstruction of ACL
tears in skeletally immature patients; however, during the 4 years postinjury, one-third
of patients required ACL reconstruction for persistent symptoms of instability, and one-
fifth of patients sustained new meniscal pathology requiring management.

Given the perils of the nonsurgical management of complete ACL tears in children and
the necessity of respecting growing physes, contemporary surgical techniques and
instrumentation offer various reconstruction options. These may be broadly categorized
as: physeal-sparing (extra-physeal and all-epiphyseal), partial transphyseal, and
transphyseal.
Recent case reports and imaging studies demonstrate the potential for variable amounts
of growth disturbance after different reconstruction techniques, some of which include
pediatric-specific modifications.33-35 These growth disturbances resulted in limb-length
discrepancy and/or angular deformity because of physeal arrest, retardation, tethering,
or overgrowth.36 The cost of delayed surgical management may be greater than the
potential growth disturbances.
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques
Complete ACL ruptures can be managed nonsurgically in sedentary patients (rare in this age
group) and those with medical comorbidities precluding safe surgical reconstruction and
recovery.
Partial ACL injuries can be selectively managed nonsurgically based on the functionality of the
partially injured ligament.

Techniques
Nonsurgical management of partial ACL injuries should be reserved for those who do
not lose native function of their ACL. An analysis of partial ACL injuries by Kocher et al37
noted that younger patients (age <14 years), smaller tear size (<50%), tears of the
anteromedial bundle, and relative stability on the pivot shift test (<grade B) were more
likely to result in adequate outcomes with nonsurgical management. Older patients with
a larger tear or tears involving the posterolateral bundle with resultant rotational
instability did not fare as well. In borderline cases, an examination under anesthesia,

with or without a diagnostic arthroscopy, may be useful to determine the final treatment
strategy.
The nonsurgical management pathway proposed by Kocher et al37 for ACL injuries in
skeletally immature patients is as follows: (1) touch-down weight-bearing restrictions for
6 to 8 weeks, then advanced as tolerated; (2) use of a hinged knee brace to prevent
hyperextension (the study protocol avoided passive terminal extension for 6 weeks and
active terminal extension for 12 weeks); (3) initiation of a physical therapy program,
focused on hamstring strengthening for dynamic support, early in the recovery process;
and (4) return to play with the use of a brace 3 months postinjury.
Complications
Nonsurgical management of the ACL-deficient knee is difficult in young, active patients
because adherence to activity modifications and bracing is unreliable in this population.
Vavken and Murray38 reviewed 47 studies on the outcomes of surgical and nonsurgical
management of ACL injuries in pediatric patients and reported that surgical reconstruction
was associated with superior outcomes with regard to patient outcomes, future instability, and
development of secondary injuries.
Studies have shown a time-sensitive effect on delayed ACL reconstruction in pediatric patients
with regard to the development of secondary injuries.39,40 Lawrence et al39 showed that
reconstruction delayed more than 12 weeks was associated with a fourfold increase in medial
meniscal tears, a 5.6-fold increase in medial compartment chondral injury, and an 11.5-fold
increase in lateral compartment chondral injury. The authors also noted a continuous time-
dependent relationship between surgical delay and the development of medial meniscal or
lateral/patellofemoral chondral injuries.
A recent series noted a 6% increased risk of meniscal tear per month of ACL reconstruction
delay.13
Surgical Management
Indications

Surgical management is indicated for most ACL ruptures, given the complications associated
with nonsurgical management.
A rupture that disrupts the physiologic function of the ACL is an indication for surgical
management.

Indications
Given the potential complications of delayed surgical management and the lower
efficacy of nonsurgical management, most ACL ruptures should be managed surgically. A
rupture should be managed if it affects the typical physiologic function of the ACL.
Preoperative Planning
ACL reconstruction techniques are selected based on multiple considerations for each
individual patient, including age (chronologic and skeletal), sex, and anticipated growth
remaining.

Preoperative Planning
Because skeletal age is a readily quantifiable marker of skeletal maturation, it is heavily
relied on in determining the best surgical technique for skeletally immature patients.
Prepubescent patients with considerable growth remaining (Tanner stage 1 or stage 2;
skeletal age =11 years in girls or =12 years in boys) typically are treated via a physeal-
sparing ACL reconstruction technique (iliotibial band reconstruction or all-epiphyseal
reconstruction).41,42 Pubescent patients with growth remaining (Tanner stage =3;
skeletal age =12 years in girls or =13 years in boys) typically are treated via a physeal-
respecting ACL reconstruction technique, which involves transphyseal tunnel placement
on the femur and/or tibia, soft-tissue autografting (hamstring or quadriceps), and
metaphyseal fixation that does not cross the physes.43

Iliotibial band reconstruction

Physeal-Sparing ACL Reconstruction
In prepubescent children (Tanner stage 1 or 2; skeletal age =11 years in girls or =12 years
in boys), modified MacIntosh combined extra-articular and intra-articular ACL
reconstruction with iliotibial band autografting as described by Micheli et al41 and
Kocher et al42 provides a stable knee without the creation of osseous tunnels. In this
reconstruction technique, the central portion of the iliotibial band is harvested
proximally and left attached to the Gerdy tubercle distally. The graft is brought through
the knee in an over-the-top-position posteriorly and passed under the intermeniscal

ligament anteriorly within an epiphyseal groove on the tibia. The graft is fixed with the
use of suture to the intermuscular septum and the periosteum on the femur and the
periosteum on the tibia. This technique is associated with the advantages of avoiding the
physes, improving the ease of revision surgery (no previous tunnels and all other
autograft sources remain intact), and providing an additional extra-articular
reconstruction limb analogous to the anterolateral ligament.42,44-46 Some opponents of
this technique cite its nonanatomic configuration; however, biomechanical studies have
shown restoration of kinematic constraint.47
The re-tear rate in a cohort of 44 patients (mean age, 10.3 years; mean follow-up, 5.3
years) was 4.5%; in patients with intact grafts at follow-up, the mean International Knee
Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective knee score was 96.7 ± 6.0 and the mean
Lysholm Knee Scale score was 95.7 ± 6.7.42 All patients were able to return to their
preoperative sporting activities, and no clinical or radiographic growth disturbances
were noted. These results also have been maintained in the longer term, with a
subsequent study of 237 patients reporting a 5.8% revision rate, 2.1% arthrofibrosis rate,
and no limb length or angular deformities at a mean follow-up of 6.2 years. Mean
pediatric IKDC and Lysholm Knee scale scores were 93 points each.48

All-Epiphyseal ACL Reconstruction
The all-epiphyseal technique, originally described by Anderson49 and modified by others,
involves the use of a soft-tissue autograft (hamstring or quadriceps) and all-epiphyseal
sockets with suspensory epiphyseal fixation.50-52 The tunnels in the all-epiphyseal
technique are drilled under fluoroscopic guidance, with care to avoid injury to the physis.
Grafts can be prepared with pre-tensioning and circumferential compression to limit
tunnel diameter and preserve bone in small, developing knees.53
In his original series, Anderson49 reported on 12 prepubescent patients (mean age, 13.3
years). The mean IKDC scores was 96.5 and side-to-side KT-1000 arthrometer difference
was 1.5 mm at a mean follow-up of 4.1 years, without any substantial length or angular
limb deformity. Cassard et al54 noted 100% return to activities in a series of 28 subjects
at a follow-up of 2.8 years; however, this outcome was not reported in other studies.
Complications have been reported in the orthopaedic literature, which mainly consists of

Physeal-Respecting ACL Reconstruction
In borderline pubescent children who are nearing skeletal maturity but have limited
remaining growth (eg, Tanner stage 3), partial transphyseal reconstruction has been
described.56,57 In this technique, a physeal-avoiding over-the-top position or all-
epiphyseal femoral tunnel is used in combination with a transphyseal, vertical, centrally
located tibial tunnel. This technique aims to avoid injury to the lateral distal femoral
physis and resultant angular deformity while minimizing changes to tibial tunnel
preparation.

Few small series have demonstrated clinical outcomes via this technique, with no
substantial length or angular deformity but graft rupture and subsequent
cartilage/meniscal injury rates of 20% to 25%, respectively.56,57
In older children and adolescents with some growth remaining (Tanner stage 1 or 2;
skeletal age ≤11 years in girls or ≤12 years in boys), safe transphyseal reconstruction
may be performed by removing an acceptable amount of physeal tissue and using soft-
tissue grafts with metaphyseal fixation.43,58,59 Animal studies indicate that removal of
less than 7% of the area of the physeal plate is not associated with an increased risk of
growth disturbance; however, the applicability of these data to humans remains
uncertain.60-62 In this technique, the tibial and femoral tunnels are created in the
standard, transphyseal fashion with care taken to violate as little physeal tissue as
possible to avoid growth disturbance. Techniques for femoral tunnel preparation are
controversial, with some studies advocating a more vertical tunnel to minimize physeal
injury. Advantages of anatomic restoration of the femoral ACL footprint likely outweigh
the potential risks of physeal injury.
Several studies have shown early (2 to 4 years) improvements in patient-reported
outcomes with IKDC and Lysholm Knee Scale scores in the 90s,20,33,63-67 which have
been maintained at follow-up as long as 6 to 10 years postoperatively.51,65 Leg-length
discrepancy has been reported in as many as 30% of patients; however, it rarely exceeds
1 cm.20,26,33,63-65,68 Typically, a low rate of revision surgery (zero to 14%) is reported,
with revision surgery often necessary because of reinjury after return to full sports
participation.14,26,69
Postoperative Management/Rehabilitation

Postoperative Management/Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation is largely similar for all ACL reconstruction techniques. The iliotibial band
ACL technique, because of its periosteal fixation, requires weight-bearing and motion
restrictions for the first 6 weeks postoperatively. After 6 weeks, all rehabilitation

protocols consist of progression to full range of motion and closed chain strengthening,
with a progressive return-to-running program initiated at approximately 3 months
postoperatively.
Higher-level activities, such as plyometrics and agility work, are initiated at 6 months
postoperatively, and patients are steadily progressed toward sport-specific training and
jump-landing. Patients are evaluated via an ACL return-to-play assessment at 9 months
postoperatively; this includes evaluation of range of motion, strength, thigh girth, and
balance, as well as functional testing. Patients wear a functional ACL brace during
exercise and sports activity for as many as 2 years postoperatively. Bracing is optional
after 2 years postoperatively; however, it is encouraged for younger, prepubescent
patients and those who compete in high-risk sports. Patients typically are followed via
annual clinical examinations until skeletal maturity to ensure lower-extremity growth is
progressing in a normal fashion. Alignment radiographs are not routinely obtained but
are useful in patients in whom growth disturbances are suspected.
Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
Most posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries in skeletally immature patients can be managed
nonsurgically.
PCL injuries requiring surgical stabilization should strive for all-epiphyseal fixation on the
femur while minimizing disruption of the tibial physis.

Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
Isolated injuries to the PCL are rare in skeletally immature patients, and sparse literature
is available to dictate management.70 In general, most PCL injuries can be managed
nonsurgically, and long-term symptomatic instability is rare. In patents with considerable
instability (grade 3 posterior drawer tests, quadriceps active test), surgical reconstruction
may be considered.71 All-epiphyseal fixation on the medial femoral condyle is typically

Pearls and Pitfalls
Accurate determination of projected future skeletal growth is essential in the
development of a treatment plan for young patients with an ACL injury. In females, a
menstruation history may be very helpful because it is a sign of impending physeal
closure and the cessation of growth. In all patients, determination of skeletal age via a
bone age radiograph is the most reliable means of quantifying future skeletal growth. In
general, for patients with substantial expected growth remaining (girls ≤11 years or boys
≤12 years), a surgical technique that avoids any physeal disruption is advocated (iliotibial
band or all-epiphyseal techniques). For patients with moderate expected growth
remaining (girls ≥12 years or boys ≥13 years), a more traditional reconstruction
technique involving transphyseal bone tunnels with soft-tissue grafts and metaphyseal
fixation is advocated.
Preoperative imaging studies should include long-leg alignment radiographs. Genu
valgum is a condition that predisposes patients to ACL injury, and it also is a
documented iatrogenic complication of ACL reconstruction in skeletally immature
patients. Preoperative imaging studies allow for early identification of pathologic genu
valgum, enabling consideration of guided growth procedures at the time of ACL
reconstruction. Routine postoperative alignment imaging studies allow for accurate
tracking of alignment changes in patients who undergo surgical reconstruction to
identify alterations in growth patterns in a timely fashion.
